records.summary: Bravard, Goichot and Gaillot surveyed aggregate operators along the Lower Mekong in Lao PDR, Thailand, Cambodia and Viet Nam. records.title: The Viet Nam Mekong Delta Sand Budget
records.authors: Project partners led by Deltares, supported by WWF
records.dateEvidence: No reliable publication date identified on the project page. The project period is not used as a publication date.
records.studyPeriod: 2022–2023 project; observations from 2022 and a vision to 2040
records.location: Viet Nam Mekong Delta
records.summary: The project page describes a delta-wide sand budget combining field measurements, numerical modelling and stakeholder consultation. It reports extraction of roughly 35–55 million m³/year, against incoming sand flux of 2–4 million m³/year and natural outgoing flux of 0–0.6 million m³/year. records.location: Vientiane Capital, Lao PDR (meeting); sand mining along the Mekong River and its tributaries in Lao PDR
records.summary: On 2 February 2026 in Vientiane, partners in the WWF-Laos and Lao Academy of Social and Economic Sciences project "Safeguarding the Mekong: Advancing Sand Governance and Biodiversity Protection for Climate Resilience in Laos" held a roundtable to present initial research findings on sand mining policies and practices along the Mekong River and its tributaries in Lao PDR. The project is supported by the CARA initiative with UK FCDO funding. According to the article, initial findings and rapid assessments highlighted growing environmental pressures, including riverbank erosion, habitat degradation, biodiversity impacts and potential risks to community livelihoods. Desk reviews identified policy and regulatory gaps, particularly in implementation, coordination and enforcement. Next steps include continued research, awareness-raising, national dialogues, policy briefs and regional knowledge-sharing workshops.

records.title: From Tibet to the 'Nine Dragons', Vietnam's Mekong Delta Is Losing Sand
records.dateKind: Publication date stated in article body
records.location: Mo Cay and Ben Tre province, Mekong Delta, Vietnam; Reuters visited three provinces straddling different branches of the delta
records.summary: Reuters reports that upstream damming and extensive riverbed sand mining are causing the land in the Mekong Delta to sink at around 2 cm (0.75 inches) a year, according to experts and officials. Riverbank erosion in Ben Tre province has destroyed homes, such as that of shopkeeper Ta Thi Kim Anh. Can Tho University expert Duong Van Ni says the problem is a lack of sediment and that since China built hydropower plants new sand almost never reaches the delta. The article says sand mining in Cambodia boomed over the last 10 years, partly driven by Singapore demand, and Cambodia banned all sand exports in 2017 under pressure from environmental groups. In Ben Tre, officials describe night-time illegal miners, and a local patrol group claims it got rid of 90 percent of thieves in the first few months, with none approaching since 2018. China's Foreign Ministry and Singapore's Ministry of National Development gave statements on downstream concerns and import controls respectively.

mergedLocalRecords.title: Morphological changes in the lower Lancang River due to extensive human activities
mergedLocalRecords.authors: Peijia Wang, Kaidao Fu, Jiangcheng Huang, Xingwu Duan and Zaizhi Yang
mergedLocalRecords.location: Jinghong to Guanlei reach, including Jinghongba and Ganlanba reaches, Yunnan, China
mergedLocalRecords.summary: Using multi-source satellite imagery (1993–2016) and a November 2018 field survey between Jinghong and Guanlei in Yunnan, the authors identified six sand-mining sites (three in Ganlanba, two large sites in Guanlei, and one in Jinghong halted after 2008). They report 1993–2016 erosion areas of 0.36 km² in Jinghongba and 0.33 km² (against 0.61 km² accretion) in Ganlanba, concluding that cascade dams reduced upstream sediment supply so sand-mining pits could not refill, accelerating bed deepening, particle coarsening and beach erosion.
mergedLocalRecords.limitations: The study maps six mining sites and planform changes in Yunnan but does not quantify annual extracted sand volumes; observed morphological changes reflect interacting effects of cascade dams, channel regulation and riverbed mining.

records.title: Stop sand mining to save the Mekong Delta
records.dateKind: publisher datePublished metadata and body date
records.location: Mekong Delta (ĐBSCL), Vietnam, including Tien River in Dong Thap, Vam Nao River in Cho Moi, An Giang, and Hau River
records.summary: Tuổi Trẻ reports on a workshop held 16 June organised by the Vietnam Hydraulic Association and the HCMC Hydraulic Science Association. Papers reportedly agreed on recommending an end to sand mining in the Mekong Delta; delegates said that without stopping it the delta would be in danger within a few decades. A Marine Engineering Institute report said that since 2005 erosion on the Tien River in Dong Thap has been intense; Đỗ Hoài Nam stated that 101 km of the 122.9 km main channel in Dong Thap is eroded, nearly 300 ha of bank land was lost in 2005-2016, and losses were estimated at about 320 billion dong. A 24 April landslide on the Vam Nao River in Cho Moi, An Giang, reportedly destroyed 16 houses. Scientists attributed erosion to flood flows, reduced sand from upstream Mekong structures, and excessive sand mining. Research data cited say sediment reaching the delta from upstream is only about 30 million tonnes per year, while licensed sand extraction (excluding illegal mining) is reportedly comparable. Some participants proposed a total ban, while others said only reduced extraction is feasible now because of high construction demand and no substitutes.
records.limitations: News report of workshop presentations; underlying studies are not detailed, and the sediment and mining figures are cited without methodology. Licensed mining volume is only said to be roughly equal to 30 million tonnes per year, with no separate exact figure. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.title: Mekong River dry season changes due to hydropower dams and extractive processes: Making sense of contradictory community observations in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia
records.authors: Ian G. Baird, Michael A.S. Thorne and Sirasak Gaja-Svasti
records.dateEvidence: Article header lists Water Alternatives Volume 18, Issue 3 (2025), pp. 521–545; exact day not printed in the article PDF
records.studyPeriod: Focus group interviews in 44 villages (1 March–3 April 2024), follow-up interviews in May–June 2024 and May–June 2025, and gauge records spanning 1923–2023
records.location: 32 villages across 8 Thai provinces (Chiang Rai to Ubon Ratchathani), 9 villages in Champasak (Lao PDR), and 3 villages in Stung Treng (Cambodia)
records.summary: Combining March–April 2024 focus groups across 44 Mekong villages in Thailand, Lao PDR and Cambodia with gauge and sediment records, the authors explain why 17 sandy-substrate villages between Nong Khai and Mukdahan perceived lower dry-season water levels despite dam releases increasing dry-season discharge. They link the perceived drop to riverbed incision from upstream sediment trapping, bank embankments (83% of the Thai bank versus 12–13% of the Lao bank) and sand mining, noting Thai–Lao rules barring mining within 1,000 m of embankments and a Vientiane operator’s report that post-monsoon sand accumulation fell from 6 m in the early 1990s to 80 cm.
records.limitations: Full article read. The authors note that neither Thailand nor Lao PDR collects public totals of actual sand volumes extracted, and their analysis cannot quantitatively separate mining-driven incision from dam-driven hungry-water incision.

records.title: Can restoring water and sediment fluxes across a mega-dam cascade alleviate a sinking river delta?
records.authors: Samuel De Xun Chua, Yuheng Yang, G. Mathias Kondolf, Chantha Oeurng, Ty Sok, Shurong Zhang, and Lu Xixi
records.dateEvidence: PMC article header: Science Advances, 2024-05-01 Date supplied in Gemini handoff; detailed publication-date review pending.
records.location: 14 mainstream stations from Lancang cascade (China) to Vietnamese Mekong Delta
records.summary: Analyzing discharge and suspended sediment load (SSL) across 14 mainstream stations from China to the Vietnamese Mekong Delta (pre-dam <1992 vs. mega-dam 2010–2019), this study documents an 84% SSL decline at Chiang Saen (from 79.2 ± 6.2 Mt/yr to 12.5 ± 1.4 Mt/yr) and an 86.5% trapping efficiency across the 11-dam Lancang cascade (45.6 km3 total storage, 19.2 km3 dead storage). Manwan and Dachaoshan reservoirs have lost 64–90% and 52–100% of total capacity to sedimentation, respectively, while Nuozhadu's 10.4 km3 dead storage would take ~170 years to fill. Even under a 4-month maximum sluicing scenario (MaxS), VMD SSL recovers only to 62.3 ± 8.2 Mt/yr (from 43.2 ± 4.5 Mt/yr), short of the 100–160 Mt/yr pre-dam level.
records.limitations: Lancang dam operational schedules are not publicly available and had to be inferred from Chiang Saen hydrographs (2015–2019); bedload and bank-erosion sediment contributions were excluded, and downstream routing from Khong Chiam to the VMD assumed zero water/sediment loss (representing an upper-bound estimate). records.title: Planning dam portfolios for low sediment trapping shows limits for sustainable hydropower in the Mekong
records.authors: R. J. P. Schmitt, S. Bizzi, A. Castelletti, J. J. Opperman, and G. M. Kondolf
records.dateEvidence: PMC article header: Science Advances, 2019-10-23 Date supplied in Gemini handoff; detailed publication-date review pending.
records.location: Mekong River Basin (790,000 km2)
records.summary: Coupling the CASCADE sediment-routing model with the Borg multiobjective evolutionary algorithm across 124 existing and proposed large dams (59,000 MW / 268,000 GWh/yr total potential) in the 790,000 km2 Mekong Basin, this study shows that the current/under-construction dam portfolio (~125,000 GWh/yr) reduces delta sediment supply from 160 Mt/yr (pre-dam) to 52 Mt/yr. Full business-as-usual (BAU) build-out traps 95% of sediment, cutting delta delivery to ~9 Mt/yr. Strategic sequencing from the current portfolio across the whole basin (WMSP 1) could expand generation by 45% while reducing delta sediment by only 4% (to 50 Mt/yr), compared to 11 Mt/yr (-79%) under BAU 1, whereas Lower Mekong-only planning (LMSP 1) yields 165,100 GWh/yr at 42 Mt/yr sediment.
records.limitations: CASCADE omits smaller hydropower and irrigation dams (especially in Thailand), does not model transient bed/bank erosion that temporarily buffers dam trapping, excludes reservoir sediment-flushing/sluicing operations, and assumes 10% of total sediment load is sandy bedload completely trapped behind dams. records.dateEvidence: Thesis defense/publication date: 2022-08-31 Date supplied in Gemini handoff; detailed publication-date review pending.

records.summary: Using SWAT-CUP calibrated across 7 mainstream stations (1984–1998) and 17 MRC DSMP sediment stations (2009–2019) alongside GFDL RCP4.5/RCP8.5 climate projections (2020–2058) and 2000–2017 salinity/rice data across 57 VMD stations, this thesis finds that 77.7–93.5% of suspended sediment is transported during the July–October monsoon, with 2009–2013 rainy-season SSL ranging from 0.3 Mt/yr at Chiang Saen to 76.8 Mt/yr at Stung Treng (~8.5 Mt/yr contributed by the 3S catchment). records.title: Large-scale suspended sediment transport and sediment deposition in the Mekong Delta
records.publisher: Hydrology and Earth System Sciences (Copernicus Publications)
records.authors: N. V. Manh, N. V. Dung, N. N. Hung, B. Merz, H. Apel
records.dateEvidence: Published: 15 Aug 2014 (Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci., 18, 3033–3053, 2014). Date supplied by Gemini; independent date verification is pending.
records.location: Mekong Delta from Kratie (Cambodia) to the South China Sea coast, including Tonle Sap Lake and Vietnamese floodplains
records.summary: A coupled quasi-2D hydrodynamic and cohesive suspended-sediment transport model (MIKE 11) calibrated against six objective functions for the 2011 flood quantified sediment routing across the entire Mekong Delta from Kratie to the coast. Depending on flood magnitude, 48–60% of Kratie's annual sediment load reached the coast, while 19–23% deposited in Cambodian floodplains and only 1–6% in compartmented, diked Vietnamese floodplains, where associated N, P, and K nutrients still supply >50% of typical rice fertilizer needs.
records.limitations: Scarcity of in-situ sediment observations across the complex channel-floodplain network necessitated multi-zone parameter calibration, and the 1D/quasi-2D cohesive sediment formulation excludes non-cohesive bedload transport and sand mining pits. Publisher headline checked; the submitted summary awaits independent editorial verification. This contextual research does not by itself isolate the effects of sand mining.
